She still wakes up coughing at night and peak flows average 360 L/min (vs 490 L/min predicted). Her BP is 110/80 mmHg, heart rate is 75 bpm and regular, there is scattered wheeze on auscultation of the chest.

According to NICE guidelines, which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Offer a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)/formoterol combination inhaler
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Offer a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)/formoterol combination inhaler

As per the 2024 NICE/BTS/SIGN guidelines, a low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)/formoterol combination inhaler should be trialled first before considering a low dose MART.

E Add salmeterol

Salmeterol should not be considered before a low dose combination inhaler or MART.

A Add low dose oral prednisolone

Add low dose oral prednisolone, is incorrect. This should only be done if other options including increasing inhaled steroid, adding montelukast, adding theophylline if appropriate, have been exhausted first.

C Add theophylline

This is appropriate if the response to inhaled therapies and montelukast is inadequate.

D Increase inhaled steroid

Increasing inhaled steroid here is unlikely to be effective and not as per the guidelines.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old man presents with left-sided pleuritic chest pain. It had come on suddenly three days previously. Initially, he thought it was secondary to his workout in the gym. However, since it did not improve and he noticed that he was slightly more breathless than usual, he went to the Emergency Department. He has no significant past medical history. He is a smoker. On examination, he looked well. He was a tall, thin man and was not short of breath at rest. Examination was unremarkable except for a clicking sound which was synchronous with the heart sounds. CXR was unremarkable.

How would you best manage this patient?
options: Analgesia and discharge with follow-up in the clinic
Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and admit patient
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Analgesia and discharge with follow-up in the clinic

A synchronous click with the heart sounds is a recognised sign of a small left apical pneumothorax. He is a tall thin man and a smoker, which are both risk factors for developing a pneumothorax. There is a strong association between pneumothoraces and smoking. The most recent British Thoracic Society (BTS) guidelines suggest that if the postero-anterior (PA) chest X-ray is normal and a small pneumothorax is suspected, a lateral decubitus chest X-ray provides added information in up to 14% of cases. Expiratory films add little and are not recommended. The treatment of a primary pneumothorax in a non-smoker with no evidence of underlying lung disease less than 50 years old with a rim of air of less than 2 cm and no breathlessness is to discharge and follow up as an outpatient. Although this patient is a smoker there is nothing to suggest underlying lung disease and it is likely that his apical pneumothorax is too small to safely aspirate. Patients should be given analgesia if required and clear instructions to return if their symptoms get any worse.

Management of spontaneous pneumothorax: British Thoracic Society pleural disease guideline 2010 | Thorax (bmj.com)

E Refer to Cardiology Department

This would not be helpful in diagnosing pneumothorax.

B Aspiration of chest

There is no clinical indication to admit this patient, although he should be followed up as an outpatient.

C Chest drain insertion

There is no indication to aspirate a small pneumothorax in a young patient with no lung disease who is not breathless when reviewed.

D Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and admit patient

There is no indication insert a chest drain in a small pneumothorax in a young patient with no lung disease who is not breathless when reviewed.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman undergoes routine cholecystectomy. Her preoperative full blood count was normal and her operative progress was unremarkable other than a small postoperative bleed that settled with simple pressure to the wound. You are asked to see her, as she has become confused. She has no previous medical history of note and works as a computer programmer. On examination, she is disorientated in time and place. Temperature 37.9 °C, pulse 110 beats per minute (bpm), blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. Heart sounds are normal and jugular venous pressure is not raised. Chest reveals some bronchial breathing on the right lower and middle zones. Her O₂ saturation is 91% on air. Abdominal examination reveals mild tenderness around the operative scar but is otherwise normal.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)95 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)12.3 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 x 10 9/l
Platelets (PLT)790 ×10⁹/L150–400 x 10 9/l
Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.5 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)197 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
C-reactive Protein (CRP)272 mg/L< 10 mg/L

A blood film shows a dramatic increase in platelets with many enlarged forms. There is an increase in left- shifted granulocytes including metamyelocytes, myelocytes and promyelocytes.

In addition to basic resuscitation, what action would you take?
options: Aspirin 300 mg with ceftazidime 1 g twice daily intravenously
Aspirin 75 mg plus hydroxyurea 1 g twice daily
Apheresis to reduce the platelet count urgently
Anticoagulation with heparin to therapeutic levels
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Broad spectrum antibiotic intravenously

This patient has developed postoperative pneumonia, which is making her confused secondary to hypoxia. The platelet count is raised secondary to infection – the normal preoperative count makes a primary haematological diagnosis unlikely in the extreme; the left shift is also secondary to infection. First-line therapy in this situation depends upon the presence or absence of risk factors for multi-drug resistant pathogens, knowledge of the local predominant pathogens and the patient's prior microbiology results. Additional consideration for treating anaerobic bacteria must be made if aspiration pneumonia is a possibility.

C Apheresis to reduce the platelet count urgently

Given that the platelet count increase is reactive as a result of ongoing infection, there is no indication for apheresis to take place.

A Aspirin 300 mg with ceftazidime 1 g twice daily intravenously

Aspirin is not required in this situation given that the increased platelet count is reactive; ceftazidime is an appropriate antibiotic choice where Pseudomonas is suspected.

B Aspirin 75 mg plus hydroxyurea 1 g twice daily

Hydroxyurea with aspirin is standard treatment for essential thrombocytosis, a clonal stem cell disorder associated with increased risk of thrombosis and haemorrhage.

D Anticoagulation with heparin to therapeutic levels

Anticoagulation with heparin to therapeutic levels isn’t indicated, and may in the postoperative period increase the risk of haemorrhage. Prophylactic dosing with low-molecular weight heparin may, however, be used here.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old woman comes to the Respiratory Clinic for review. She has been suffering from asthma, confirmed by her general practitioner (GP) on peak flow testing, for the past four years. She has progressively increased her therapy to cope with symptoms of wheeze, shortness of breath on exercise and nocturnal coughing, but she is still not controlled. A past history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (AF) is noted, although she is currently not using any medication for prophylaxis. Current asthma medication includes inhaled beclometasone 400 mg twice daily and montelukast 10 mg orally (she originally responded well to the introduction of the oral therapy). On examination, her blood pressure is 115/85 mmHg and pulse 75 bpm and regular. There is bilateral wheeze on auscultation. Peak flow is 390 litres/minute (500 litres/minute predicted).

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Inhaled salmeterol

The updated 2024 guidelines from NICE, SIGN, and BTS recommend adding a LABA, such as salmeterol, to the existing inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) therapy for patients aged 12 and over who are not achieving control with medium-dose ICS and a leukotriene receptor antagonist. This approach aims to improve symptom control and reduce exacerbations.

E Oral Theophylline

Theophylline can be considered in certain cases but is associated with potential side effects and drug interactions. Given the patient's history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, theophylline may increase the risk of arrhythmias and is not the preferred next step.

A Inhaled Tiotropium

Tiotropium is a long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) primarily used in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). While it can be considered as an add-on therapy in certain cases of asthma, current guidelines prioritize the addition of a long-acting beta2 agonist (LABA) for patients not controlled on medium-dose ICS and a leukotriene receptor antagonist.

C Oral Prednisolone

Oral corticosteroids are generally reserved for acute exacerbations or severe asthma due to potential systemic side effects. In this scenario, other treatment options should be optimized before considering oral prednisolone.

D Oral Sodium chromoglicate

Sodium cromoglicate is less commonly used in adult asthma management and is not a preferred add-on therapy in the current guidelines. 39176

questions.question:
A 42-year-old homeless man is admitted with confusion, fever and shortness of breath. He is well known to the Emergency Department and has presented on a number of occasions with alcohol intoxication. On examination he is pyrexial at 38.6°C. He has a cough productive of purulent and blood-stained sputum. Auscultation of the chest reveals findings consistent with right-sided consolidation. His chest X-ray shown below.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Klebsiella pneumoniae

This patient has pneumonia with evidence of lung abscess formation. Given his history of alcoholism and the fact there is evidence of cavitation in the right upper lobe on chest X-ray, Klebsiella is a likely cause. Third- generation cephalosporins or quinolones provide coverage for community-acquired infection but macrolides do not. Mortality is particularly high in patients with a history of alcoholism, potentially as a result of poor nutrition and defective immunity associated with chronic excess alcohol consumption.

Image source: http://www.svuhradiology.ie/case-study/cavitating-pneumonia/

A Chlamydia psittaci

C. psittaci is associated with atypical pneumonia as a result of exposure to infected birds. Symptoms may initially mimic typhoid fever with fever, joint pains, gastrointestinal (GI) disturbance, headache and lymphopaenia. A cough and evidence of respiratory tract infection develop later.

B Haemophilus influenzae

H. influenzae infection is associated primarily with exacerbations of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) rather than the cavitating pneumonia seen here.

D Staphylococcus aureus

S. aureus is also associated with cavitation and abscess formation, but occurs more commonly after an episode of influenza.

E Streptococcus pneumoniae

S. pneumoniae is a common cause of community-acquired pneumonia, although it is not usually cavitating.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old computer software firm owner presents with increasing breathlessness over the past few months. He has previously been fit and well and had installed a home gym, swimming pool and hot tub/steam room to use for personal training around 18 months ago. He is a non-smoker and has a previous history of asthma as a child. Examination reveals crackles and high-pitched wheeze throughout the lung fields. His blood pressure is 115/75 mmHg, with pulse 70 and regular. There is no ankle swelling.

Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention in this case?
options: Repainting and ventilation in the steam room
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Repainting and ventilation in the steam room

Treatment of hypersensitivity pneumonitis (the diagnosis in this case) centres on allergen avoidance. Cladosporum is found in association with ceiling mould and is a source of ‘hot-tub lung’; as such, it is the most likely cause of his symptoms. Other moulds known to lead to hypersensitivity include micropolyspora, Aspergillus and thermoactinomycetes, which are associated with mouldy hay, mushroom compost and contaminated water in humidifiers. Trichosporum is associated with house dust. In this case the likely source is the steam room, and hence repainting and adequate ventilation should prevent further exposure.

E Oral antibiotics

Oral antibiotics have no role in the treatment of hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

A Inhaled corticosteroids

Inhaled corticosteroids are ineffective in the treatment of hypersensitivity pneumonitis; removal of exposure to the precipitant allergen is the most important intervention.

B Oral corticosteroids

Oral corticosteroids may be given for an initial period to kick-start the recovery in symptoms. However, if strict allergen avoidance is not practised, his symptoms will not completely resolve.

C Oral antifungals

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is related to exposure to antigen rather than invasive fungal disease, and hence removal of exposure is the most important intervention.

questions.question:
A 38-year-old woman underwent a heart and lung transplantation for pulmonary hypertension. Whilst she was initially well post surgery she presents to the clinic some 15 months later with progressive shortness of breath. On examination her BP is 125/82 mmHg and there is wheeze on auscultation of her chest.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin121 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)4.9 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets184 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)140 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.0 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea6.9 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine120 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L

Pulmonary function tests:

InvestigationResult
Pulmonary function testsObstructive picture, irreversible with salbutamol, worsening over the past 3 months

Pulmonary function tests irreversible with salbutamol,

worsening over the past 3 months

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome

Bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome occurs due to progressive obliterative bronchiolitis affecting terminal bronchioles. The condition is manifest in increasing shortness of breath and a progressively worsening fixed airways obstruction picture on pulmonary function testing. Risk factors for the development of the condition include early acute rejection and CMV infection. Bronchiolitis obliterans has been seen as early as 3 months post-transplant, and is responsible for over 50% of deaths after the first year.

Pulmonary hypertension (PAH) is defined by a mean pulmonary artery pressure greater than 25 mmHg at rest and a normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure of 15 mmHg or less with a pulmonary vascular resistance greater than 3 Wood units. Prior to lung transplantation being available, median survival for patients with pulmonary hypertension was 2.8 years.

A Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder

In this condition there is controlled B-cell proliferation due to the need for immunosuppressive therapy after transplantation. The clinical presentation can vary from simple lymphoid hyperplasia to aggressive disease that closely resembles non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder is still a rare disease, despite being more commonly observed after lung transplantation than with other organs.

B Acute rejection

Acute rejection may occur any time from the first week after the transplant to 3 months afterwards. All recipients have some amount of acute rejection.

D New-onset asthma

In asthma, you would see obstructive spirometry, but you would expect reversibility with salbutamol.

E Recurrence of pulmonary hypertension

Recurrence of the disease is rare after transplantation.

questions.question:
A known asthmatic is admitted to A&E with wheeze and shortness of breath, although she is not yet showing signs of fatigue. She is given continued nebulised salbutamol, IV steroids and high-flow oxygen. You are asked by the nursing sister in charge whether giving IV magnesium is appropriate.

According to the BTS guidelines, which of the following would count against the need for IV magnesium at this stage?
options: Magnesium is at the lower end of the normal range
Tachycardia with a heart rate of 120 beats/min
Patient is treated with oral theophylline
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E PEFR 240 vs 140 on admission (normal 500)

The British Thoracic Society (BTS) guidelines say that 50% magnesium sulphate at 1.2–2 g (4–8 mmol) over 20 min can be given IV to a patient with severe asthma not responding to inhaled bronchodilator or who has severe life-threatening asthma. In this case the PEFR is improving, without signs of fatigue, and it is therefore appropriate to continue with current management.

A Patient is 18 years old

Age is irrelevant when considering the need for magnesium infusion, and there is little difference in response as age increases.

B Magnesium is at the lower end of the normal range

Magnesium concentration is irrelevant as supra-therapeutic levels are given to achieve a pharmacological response with reduced acetylcholine release and improved smooth muscle relaxation

C Tachycardia with a heart rate of 120 beats/min

Heart rate >110/min is an indicator of severe asthma and more likely to drive the use of magnesium.

D Patient is treated with oral theophylline

The need for oral theophylline implies a poor response to beta-agonist therapy, and therefore a possible greater need for acute intervention with magnesium.

questions.question:
A previously well 23-year-old student presents to the Emergency Department with an acute onset of pleuritic chest pain and dyspnoea. She has just returned from a gap year to Australia and had been well until the morning of admission.

She has no significant past medical history or family history, and her only medication included the contraceptive pill. She is a non-smoker.

On examination, she is acutely distressed, with a respiratory rate of 32 breaths/min, a pulse of 128 bpm and a blood pressure of 98/60 mmHg. She is peripherally cool. Her chest is clear to auscultation, and her heart sounds are normal. The jugular venous pressure (JVP) is elevated. There is no obvious leg swelling.

Investigation results are below:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)152 g/L115 - 155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)14 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)310 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)136 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.2 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea3.2 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)90 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L

Chest X-ray Normal

Electrocardiogram is shown below

Arterial blood gases (on 15 l/min oxygen) were:

InvestigationResult
pH7.48
pa(O₂)8.2 kPa
pa(CO₂)3.6 kPa

Intravenous (IV) heparin is commenced.

Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Limited IV crystalloid fluid

The diagnosis is an acute major pulmonary embolism. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia, the commonest ECG finding in such a presentation. With a low-normal blood pressure, fluids should be given in the first instance to increase the right ventricular filling pressure and maintain cardiac output (see ESC guidelines). Heparinisation should prevent the occurrence of further emboli.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sinustachycardia_(CardioNetworks_ECGpedia).jpg (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sinustachycardia_(CardioNetworks_ECGpedia).jpg)

D IV doxapram

The use of doxapram is not indicated in this scenario. Doxapram is a respiratory stimulant, which can lead to an increase in tidal volume and respiratory rate in patients with respiratory failure. It may be useful for treating respiratory depression in patients who have taken excessive doses of opiates and failed to respond adequately to treatment with naloxone.

B Thrombolysis with streptokinase

Thrombolysis should be considered if the patient is not improving after 15–30 min with the above measures. The British Thoracic Society guidelines do not deliver any strong guidance with respect to thrombolysis, except that it should be considered where there is circulatory collapse. Pulmonary embolectomy should only be undertaken when thrombolysis is contraindicated. The diagnosis of pulmonary embolism is made by computed tomography (CT) or ventilation–perfusion (V/Q) scan.

C IV dobutamine

If hypotension is severe and does not respond to plasma expanders, inotropic support with agents such as dobutamine may be necessary.

E IV dopamine

Dopamine is not indicated in the management of this patient. There is, however, some evidence that it may be beneficial in patients with pulmonary embolism, a low cardiac index and a normal blood pressure.

questions.question:
A 69-year-old female was taken to the Emergency Department with a reduced GCS score; no history was available from relatives for the patient in A&E. The ambulance crew said that the call was put out by her husband as she had become increasingly short of breath. When they arrived she looked breathless and cyanosed. She denied any chest pain at that time. On examination he had a GCS score of 10 (M5, V2, E3), respiratory rate 10/min, BP 130/70 mmHg, pulse 120/min, temperature 36.9°C, SaO₂ 94% on 15 l oxygen. Auscultation of the chest revealed an expiratory wheeze throughout.

Heart sounds were normal and abdominal examination unremarkable. There was no obvious focal neurological abnormality and both plantars showed a flexor response.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)173 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)8.2 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)400 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)84 fl80 - 100 fl
C-reactive protein (CRP)21 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Electrocardiogram (ECG)Sinus tachycardia

In her notes you find a flow-volume curve from 1 year ago shown below.

Her chest x-ray is shown below.

ABGs on high-flow oxygen on this admission:

InvestigationResult
pH7.29
PCO₂10.91 kPa
PO₂12.39 kPa
Bicarbonate40.6 mmol/L
Base excess10.4

What does the arterial blood gas analysis show?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Acute on chronic respiratory acidosis

This patient has an acute on chronic respiratory acidosis. The high bicarbonate and base excess show that there is an underlying chronic respiratory acidosis with renal compensation. The acidosis and high CO₂ indicate an acute respiratory acidosis. If this was acute without a chronic element then, for a PCO₂ of 10.91 one would expect the pH to be lower.

The diagnosis of COPD is suggested from the CXR, showing hyperexpansion and flattened diaphragms, and flow-volume curve, which shows the classic shape for COPD. In some patients with COPD, respiratory drive depends on their degree of hypoxia, rather than the usual dependence on hypercapnia. Although it is important to prevent life-threatening hypoxia, uncontrolled oxygen therapy should be used with caution. This patient has a suppressed respiratory drive and carbon dioxide narcosis secondary to high-flow oxygen. She was able to tell the ambulance crew that she had no chest pain at home; she was then given high-flow oxygen and her GCS dropped. Note on arrival at the Emergency Department that she scored 2/5 for verbal response and therefore would not be able to give any information. The immediate management is therefore to reduce the inspired oxygen concentration and repeat the arterial blood gases. If by doing this the patient becomes hypoxic or remains acidotic, they should then be referred for non-invasive ventilation.

Image source: https://radiopaedia.org/cases/emphysema-9?lang=gb

A Mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis

The ABG would be expected to show low bicarbonate and base excess if a metabolic component to the acidosis were present.

B Acute respiratory acidosis

In acute respiratory acidosis, one would expect the bicarbonate and base excess to be lower. The raised bicarbonate implies a chronicity to the respiratory acidosis with renal compensation.

C Metabolic acidosis

The raised CO₂ implies a respiratory component to the acidosis. In a metabolic acidosis, the bicarbonate and base excess would be expected to be low.

E Metabolic alkalosis

The ABG demonstrates a low pH and raised CO₂, neither of which is in keeping with metabolic alkalosis. The bicarbonate and base excess are raised, likely representing renal compensation to a chronic respiratory acidosis.

questions.question: A 20-year-old man has recently started work in the bakery section of his local supermarket. He complains of increasing shortness of breath, cough and wheeze during the course of the working week. These symptoms resolve somewhat at weekends and improved markedly during a week’s holiday in Spain. Examination in the clinic on a Monday morning reveals no evidence of wheeze; peak flow is 520 (540 predicted). Which of the following initial actions is most appropriate in this case?
options: 2-hourly peak flow recordings during the week, comparing work to rest periods
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B 2-hourly peak flow recordings during the week, comparing work to rest periods

It is important to establish the relationship of deterioration in peak flow to work periods as there is a suspicion of occupational asthma here. Occupational asthma in bakers may occur due to flour dust or to other allergens used in making breads and cakes. Review of the worker’s work pattern, allowing for removal of exposure to the potential allergen, is optimal therapy, of course with the cooperation of the employer.

D Bronchial provocation testing

Bronchial provocation testing should only be undertaken in specialised centres, with appropriate anaesthetist support, and only when there is doubt as to the underlying trigger.

A Trial of salbutamol

A trial of salbutamol is inappropriate given the likely history of occupational triggers for this patient’s asthma. Removal of exposure to any potential allergen is much more important than starting asthma therapy.

C CXR

A CXR is not useful when evaluating potential bronchoconstriction related to asthma.

E Patch testing

Patch testing is rarely useful in evaluating occupational asthma.

questions.question:
A 27-year-old woman is referred to the Emergency Department for sudden development of shortness of breath, with left-sided chest pains but no cough or haemoptysis. She is 28 weeks into an uneventful pregnancy.

On examination, she appears anxious; her BP is 110/60 mmHg, heart rate 92 bpm and respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute. Her oxygen saturation on air is 98%. Her chest is clinically clear. Her cardiovascular and lower limb examinations are unremarkable.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)113 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)10.1 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)278 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.5 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)112 µmol/L50–120µmol/L
Urea6.1 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)6 mg/L< 10 mg/L
D-dimers0.62 mg/L< 0.25 mg/L

An ECG shows sinus rhythm at 110 bpm. Which of the following investigations would be the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B CXR

This patient has symptoms of a potential pulmonary embolus, and Green-top guidance from the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG) recommends a CXR as an initial step in investigation. A D-dimer level is unreliable when measured in pregnancy and guidance does not support its use.

D CT pulmonary angiography

CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is the preferred investigation post-CXR in the event that the chest X-ray is found to be abnormal. The choice of performing either CTPA or ventilation/perfusion scan (V/Q) is a balance between the risk of radiation exposure to the pregnant woman’s breast tissue (much higher with CTPA) and that of radiation exposure to the fetus (which is higher with V/Q scanning).

A Bilateral lower limb Doppler scan

Given that the lower limbs appear normal on examination, a bilateral lower limb Doppler scan in this case, is unlikely to prove useful in ruling in or out a pulmonary embolus.

C Echocardiography

Echocardiography is most useful as a bedside investigation when there is a high suspicion of pulmonary embolism and the patient is unstable. It may reveal evidence of right ventricular strain. Here, the patient is stable, and therefore, echocardiography is less likely to contribute towards the diagnosis.

E Ventilation/perfusion scan

According to the RCOG guidelines, ventilation/perfusion V/Q or CTPA can be considered once a CXR has been performed, although where the CXR has proven to be abnormal, CTPA is preferred to V/Q.

questions.question:
A 58-year-old man was referred to the neurology clinic by his general practitioner with a 4-month history of progressive weakness. He described difficulty walking, with heavy, stiff legs. He had particular trouble in going upstairs and rising from a chair. He also occasionally had episodes of double vision. Apart from controlled hypertension, he had no significant past medical history. He smoked 20 cigarettes per day and drank 16 units of alcohol per week. On systems enquiry, he also admitted to weight loss of one stone, a persistent cough and a dry mouth. He reluctantly admitted that he had been having some sexual difficulties with his wife recently.

On examination, he looked reasonably well. There was no finger clubbing or lymphadenopathy. Cardiorespiratory examination revealed coarse crackles consistent with COPD, and abdominal examination was unremarkable. On neurological examination, his tone and sensation were normal, with no muscle wasting. He had predominantly proximal muscle weakness and his tendon reflexes were universally absent. Apart from mild bilateral ptosis, his cranial nerves were intact. Interestingly, his power and reflexes seemed to improve after a brief period of repetitive exercise of the affected muscle.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin140 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)5.0 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets300 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Urea5.2 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)82 fl76–98 fl
Sodium (Na⁺)130 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.6 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Bilirubin10 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)32 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Creatinine120 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Alkaline phosphatase80 IU/L30–130 IU/L
γGT42 IU/L5–30 IU/L

Which of the following investigations would be the most useful in making a diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Anti-calcium channel antibodies

This man has Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), which is associated with an underlying small cell carcinoma of the bronchus. This is a rare paraneoplastic phenomenon which can precede radiological evidence of the tumour by up to 5 years. LEMS is a presynaptic disorder of the neuromuscular junction which is caused by antibodies to the voltage-gated calcium channels of the nerve terminal, leading to failure of acetylcholine release. The clinical features are proximal muscle weakness and depressed tendon reflexes, which can return after a few minutes of muscular contraction. Autonomic symptoms are common. The diagnosis is made electrophysiologically, and auto-antibodies are found in 90% of cases. Treatment is with 3,4-diaminopyridine, prednisolone and occasionally plasma exchange.

B Serum acetylcholine receptor antibodies

ACh receptor antibodies would be part of the diagnostic testing for myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune muscle condition which is associated with fatigueability, ie power and function deteriorate with repeated testing.

A Tensilon (edrophonium) test

A tensilon test would be diagnostic for myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune muscle condition which is associated with fatigueability, ie power and function deteriorate with repeated testing.

C Muscle biopsy

A muscle biopsy would be useful in diagnosing an inflammatory or necrotising myopathy, but these diagnoses are less likely, given that testing improves with repetition in this patient, and one would expect power to decline with repeated testing in a myopathy.

E Serum creatine kinase

Raised creatine kinase is a non-specific marker of muscle damage. It can be elevated in, for example, inflammatory or necrotising myopathy, statin-induced myopathy, myocardial infarction, rhabdomyolysis or metabolic myopathy.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 3-day history of a productive cough, left- sided chest pain, fever and shortness of breath.

On examination, she is confused and febrile. Her BP is 89/60 mmHg, heart rate 102 bpm and respiratory rate 31 breaths per minute. Her oxygen saturation is 87%. She has left-sided upper lobe bronchial sounds on auscultation.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)123 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)15.1 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)178 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)133 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.2 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)112 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV)89 fl76–98 fl
Urea8.1 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
C-Reactive Protein (CRP)59 mg/L< 10 mg/L

Her CXR is shown below:

What is the next most important step in this patient’s immediate management?
options: Non-rebreather oxygen mask for delivery of fraction of inspired oxygen of 60–80%
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Non-rebreather oxygen mask for delivery of fraction of inspired oxygen of 60–80%

This patient has severe pneumonia, which has a mortality of approximately 10% in patients admitted to the hospital. Features of severity, according to the CURB-65 score, include: confusion, urea concentration greater than 7.0 mmol/L, respiratory rate over 30 breaths per minute, BP less than 90 mmHg systolic and age over 65 years. A score of greater than 2 indicates severe pneumonia. She would, of course, need IV antibiotics, fluids, oxygen and analgesia as rapidly as possible. In this situation, the most marked abnormality is the low O2 saturation, and this should therefore be addressed first. The CXR shows left upper lobe consolidation, which is in keeping with this diagnosis.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Lobaerpneumonie.jpg

A Hypertonic saline solution

This is inappropriate as there is only mild hyponatraemia, which does not need to be corrected urgently, and standard crystalloid fluids could be used for resuscitation. Hypertonic saline can be used in patients with chronic hyponatraemia who are symptomatic and with sodium levels of less than 120 mmol/L.

B IV fluids

While IV fluids should be given very urgently, it is of greater importance to ensure that the patient has good oxygenation.

D Potassium replacement

Potassium supplements should be given either as part of fluid management or with PO supplementation, but are of no immediate urgency for this patient.

E Start oral antibiotics

This would be inappropriate as the patient is septic secondary to a chest infection and needs IV antibiotics. Sepsis is defined as meeting two or more of systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) criteria with a suspected source of infection. SIRS criteria include temperature outside of 36–38 °C, heart rate greater than 90 bpm, a respiratory rate greater than 20 breaths per minute or partial pressure of carbon dioxide less than 32 mmHg and WCC outside of 4–12/mm3. This patient has at least three of these criteria.

questions.question:
A 64-year-old man with a history of two previous transient ischaemic attacks (TIAs) is admitted to the Emergency Department by ambulance. He has a history of obesity, hypertension and diabetes and smokes 20 cigarettes per day. His only drug treatment is metformin for diabetes. His wife called the ambulance because he fell asleep while watching a drama and was snoring loudly and she was unable to wake him. Apparently, he has recently given up driving because he feels too tired to drive any distance at all. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 155/85 mmHg and a pulse of 80 bpm and regular. He has wheeze on auscultation of the chest, but no focal signs, and his saturations are 92% on air. His body mass index (BMI) is 35 kg/m 2. Neurological examination is normal.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)133 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)8.0 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)191 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)137 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine132 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Glucose11.2 mmol/L3.5–5.5 mmol/L
HbA1c66 mmol/mol (8.2%)< 53 mmol/mol (< 7.0%)

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Sleep apnoea

The history of increasing tiredness, coupled with morbid obesity, is suggestive of sleep apnoea, with episodes of daytime sleepiness well recognised to occur in situations such as TV watching and while driving the car. A sleep study incorporating monitoring for apnoeic episodes is the obvious next step. If sleep apnoea is proven and is moderate to severe, then overnight continuous positive airways pressure (CPAP) is the initial intervention of choice. For mild sleep apnoea, a mandibular advancement device may be an appropriate alternative. Over the long term, weight reduction may lead to a regression of symptoms.

E Transient global amnesia

A significant period of amnesia without other neurological features, followed by complete recovery, is most suggestive of transient global amnesia. In addition, the condition is not thought to be associated with vascular risk factors.

A Epileptic seizure

The lack of motor features and other signs of epilepsy, including tongue biting and loss of continence, counts against epilepsy as the underlying diagnosis.

B Hypoglycaemia

The random glucose of 11.2 mmol/L and the suboptimal HbA1c control at 66 mmol/L (8.2%), coupled with use of metformin monotherapy only, rule out hypoglycaemia as a possibility.

D Transient ischaemic attack

There are no focal signs, and the features of the episode here look like more severe sleepiness against a pattern of sleep apnoea symptoms.

questions.question:
As the medical SHO, you are admitting a 22-year-old asthma patient with an exacerbation of his asthma with a cough and severe wheeze that has been worsening over the past two days. He is normally on regular, short- acting β-agonist only and his predicted peak flow is 600 l/min. You are concerned that he may need review by the intensive care team. On examination in the Emergency Department, his blood pressure (BP) is 110/72 mmHg, with pulse 110/min and regular. He has severe bilateral wheeze and his respiratory rate is 28/ min.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
PaO₂9.4 kPa10.5–13.5 kPa
PaCO₂4.4 kPa4.6–6.0 kPa
pH7.377.35–7.45
PEFR180 l/min (600 predicted)

Which of the findings is most concerning?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Peak flow of 180 l/min

The criteria for life-threatening asthma are well described in the BTS asthma guidelines. From the clinical scenario listed above, it is only his PEFR of 180 l/min which fits with those criteria, being less than 200 (33% predicted level). Given his peak flow, however, it’s obviously important that he is managed aggressively according to the guidelines, including the addition of IV magnesium if early response to nebulisers isn’t seen.

Criteria for life-threatening asthma:

PEF <33% best or predicted SpO₂ <92% PaO₂ <8 kPa Normal (or elevated) PaCO₂ (4.6–6.0 kPa) silent chest cyanosis poor respiratory effort arrhythmia

exhaustion, altered conscious level

A Respiratory rate 28/min

Monitoring respiratory rate is important in asthma even though tachypnoea is not included in the criteria for life- threatening asthma, as a fall in respiratory rate can be associated with reduced respiratory effort and exhaustion.

B Widespread wheeze

Widespread wheeze indicates good respiratory effort in an acute asthma attack. If the chest were to become silent then this would indicate life-threatening asthma.

C Heart rate 110/min

Tachycardia is an unreliable marker in asthma as it can easily occur due to repeat doses of salbutamol. However, arrhythmia implies a far worse state and should be treated quickly.

D PaCO2 4.4 kPa

Patients with exacerbation of asthma have a high respiratory rate and would be expected to have a low pCO₂ due to the increased CO₂ elimination. When CO₂ starts to rise, this implies that the patient is becoming tired and that means that the asthma can be classified as life-threatening.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man presents with progressive exertional dyspnoea and a dry cough over several months. He denies chest pain, haemoptysis, fever or weight loss. His past medical history is unremarkable, and he does not smoke. Physical examination reveals fine bibasilar crackles but no clubbing. High-resolution CT of the chest shows bilateral ground-glass opacities with interlobular septal thickening, giving a 'crazy paving' appearance. Bronchoalveolar lavage yields a milky fluid, and cytology reveals periodic acid–Schiff-positive material.

What is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Whole lung lavage

Whole lung lavage is the gold standard and first-line treatment for PAP. It involves sequentially washing out proteinaceous material from the alveoli, providing significant symptomatic relief.

E Lung transplantation

Lung transplantation is reserved for end-stage disease unresponsive to other treatments, which is rare in PAP.

A Long-term corticosteroid therapy

Corticosteroids are not the treatment of choice for autoimmune PAP and may exacerbate the condition by increasing the risk of infections.

C High-dose oxygen therapy

While oxygen therapy may be used to manage hypoxaemia, it does not address the underlying accumulation of alveolar material.

D Anti-granulocyte–macrophage colony-stimulating factor antibody therapy

Recombinant granulocyte–macrophage colony-stimulating factor therapy targets the autoimmune mechanism in pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP) and is used for refractory cases or as a second-line therapy.

questions.question:
A 54-year-old man presents to the Respiratory Clinic with his wife, who is extremely worried that he snores heavily every night and often seems to stop breathing. He also falls asleep each evening while watching the TV and has had to stop the car on a number of occasions to take a nap. He drinks two pints of beer each day and smokes five cigarettes per day. On examination, his BP is 152/85 mmHg and his heart rate is 80 bpm and regular; his BMI is elevated at 32 kg/m 2, and his collar size is 18. His Epworth score is 15. He plans to lose weight.

Which initial intervention is the most appropriate?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Continuous positive airway pressure

For patients with mild symptoms that affect their quality of life and usual daytime activities, the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines recommend fixed-level continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP). Therapy with CPAP is effective in reducing symptoms and is associated with an improvement in cardiovascular morbidity in patients with hypertension and obstructive sleep apnoea. Forty per cent of patients, however, have an elevated Epworth score after CPAP is initiated, and these individuals should, of course, be encouraged to take other measures such as losing weight.

E Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty

Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty is considered in patients who are resistant to other interventions or who have significant obstructive sleep apnoea despite weight loss.

B Gastric banding

Gastric banding would not be appropriate here as it would not treat all presentations and should be considered for patients who are unable to achieve significant weight loss.

C Mandibular advancement device

Patients with mild symptoms that affect their quality of life and usual daytime activities and who are unable to tolerate or decline to try CPAP may try a mandibular advancement device (MAD). A MAD may relieve obstruction and give this patient the opportunity to lose weight and improve his symptoms significantly. He

should, of course, also be referred for a sleep study and advised that until his symptoms significantly improve, he is not to drive. In the event that the device is ineffective and/or he fails to lose significant weight, he can be referred for an alternative management option.

D Modafinil

Modafinil would not be appropriate here as it is used to enhance wakefulness in patients with central sleep disorders.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 5-day history of shortness of breath and a cough productive of green sputum. There are no other symptoms of note and he has no past medical history. He smokes 15–20 cigarettes per day.

On examination, his Glasgow Coma Scale score is 15/15. He has a respiratory rate of 32 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturations of 91% on air. His heart sounds are normal, with a heart rate of 120 bpm and a blood pressure of 101/62 mmHg. On chest auscultation, there are coarse crackles at the left lung base.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)126 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)14.5 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils10 ×10⁹/L1.5 - 7.0 ×10⁹/L
Urea6.5 mmol/L2.5 - 6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)130 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L

Which factor in this patient’s presentation is the biggest prognostic indicator?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Respiratory rate of 32 breaths/min

This forms part of the CURB-65 criteria, an evidence-based scoring system used to estimate severity and guide management of patients with community-acquired pneumonia. The components of CURB-65 are: confusion (not present in this patient); urea concentration > 7 mmol/L (urea concentration here is < 7.0 mmol/L); respiratory rate ≥ 30 breaths/minute (this patient meets the criteria as his respiratory rate is 32 breaths per minute); systolic blood pressure < 90 mmHg (not met in this patient who has a systolic blood pressure of 110 mmHg); diastolic blood pressure < 60 mmHg; and age over 65 years (this patient is 62 years old). A CURB-65 score of zero corresponds to a 0.7% risk of mortality, whereas a score of 5 corresponds to a 57% risk. With a score of 1, this patient’s risk is 3.2%. He would be suitable for outpatient management. If he scores 2 or more, he should be managed as an inpatient.

A Age

Age of ≥ 65 years counts towards the CURB-65 criteria. This patient is 62 years old, which does score a point on this scale.

B Blood pressure

This question relates to the CURB-65 criteria – these clinical criteria provide evidence-based guidance on the severity of community-acquired pneumonia and can be used to determine the appropriate management of a patient (admission vs outpatient care, and antibiotic therapy). Blood pressure does form part of the CURB-65 criteria; however, patients score a point if their systolic blood pressure is < 90 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure is < 60 mmHg. This patient has a systolic blood pressure of 110 mmHg, and therefore, this is not the correct answer. The only criterion on which this patient scores against the CURB-65 is his respiratory rate which is ≥ 30 breaths/minute.

C Neutrophilia

Neutrophilia is not one of the features of CURB-65; the only CURB-65 criterion met by this patient is his respiratory rate which is 30 breaths per minute.

D Smoking history

Although smoking is a risk factor for more severe respiratory disease, it does not form part of the CURB-65 severity criteria for pneumonia.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old asthmatic patient presents to the Emergency Department with increasing cough and wheeze. She describes a cough productive of brown sputum. There is no other past medical history of note. She is taking a steroid inhaler regularly and increasing doses of beta-agonist, with no alleviation of her symptoms. She has worked in a bakery for many years. She is an ex-smoker and stopped smoking 20 years ago; she has a pet dog and one cat.

On examination she has a temperature of 38°C and is breathless at rest. Her BP is 122/82 mmHg, with pulse 88/min and regular. There is reduced chest expansion anteriorly on the left side, with corresponding reduced breath sounds. She has a mild expiratory wheeze.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)141 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)12.7 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils7.37 ×10⁹/L1.5–7.0 ×10⁹/L
Lymphocytes2.55 ×10⁹/L1.5–4.0 ×10⁹/L
Eosinophils2.1 ×10⁹/L0.1–0.4 ×10⁹/L
Monocytes0.6 ×10⁹/L0.0–0.8 ×10⁹/L
Basophils0.05 ×10⁹/L< 0.1 ×10⁹/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)87.3 fl80–100 fl
Platelets (PLT)314 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)28 mm/h1–20 mm/h
C-reactive protein (CRP)16 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Sodium (Na⁺)138 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.9 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Urea4.8 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine95 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Bilirubin12 µmol/L1–22 µmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)49 u/L7–55 u/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)61 u/L30–150 u/L
Albumin36 g/L35–55 g/L
X -ray scan:

CT scan on presentation:

CT scan taken one month later:

What investigation would help make a diagnosis?
options: Positive skin test/radioallergosorbent test for Aspergillus fumigatus
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Positive skin test/radioallergosorbent test for Aspergillus fumigatus

The chest X-ray shows left upper lobe collapse and demonstrates the ‘veil sign’. This patient has allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA). Pulmonary infiltrates, blood eosinophilia and asthma are usually secondary to Churg–Strauss syndrome, or allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.

ABPA is suspected in any patient with asthma who has an abnormal chest X-ray and high peripheral blood eosinophilia. The chest X-ray may show diffuse pulmonary infiltrates, and pulmonary, lobar or segmental collapse occurs as a transient feature. The most common cause is sensitivity to A. fumigatus spores.

The diagnostic criteria include:

Asthma (in most cases) Peripheral blood and sputum eosinophilia Abnormal chest X-ray (infiltrates, segmental or lobar collapse)

Positive skin tests/RAST to an extract of A. fumigatus A. fumigatus IgG serum-precipitating antibodies

Raised total IgE >1000 ng/ml Fungal hyphae of A. fumigatus on microscopy of sputum.

D Metacholine challenge test

The methacholine challenge test is used to diagnose asthma, usually where there is some doubt as to the status with respect to hyper-reactivity.

A p-ANCA

This is an appropriate test for vasculitis and is associated with Churg–Strauss syndrome. The absence of other features of vasculitis, such as mononeuritis, counts against this as the underlying diagnosis.

B c-ANCA

This is an appropriate test for vasculitis. C-ANCA positivity is associated with Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, where features such as sinusitis, haemoptysis and renal vasculitis co-exist.

E Lung function tests

Lung functions tests would not be sufficiently discriminatory to diagnose allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. They would merely demonstrate a mixed obstructive/restrictive picture.

questions.question: A 64-year-old homeless man is admitted on the routine medical take. He has lost a significant amount of weight over the past few months and now presents with increasing shortness of breath. He is a former heavy smoker. On examination: decreased air entry over the right lower chest and dullness to percussion. Chest X-ray reveals a large, right-sided pleural effusion. Pleural aspiration is performed. Which one of the following features, if present, would be the most specific indicator of probable underlying malignancy?
options: Uniform blood staining throughout pleural fluid samples
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Uniform blood staining throughout pleural fluid samples

Uniform blood staining and a protein level of >30 g/L are supportive of a diagnosis of malignancy.

pH can also be useful for interpreting pleural fluid results. Low pleural fluid pH is associated with a number of conditions, including pleural infection and empyema, inflammatory effusions such as those related to rheumatoid arthritis, tuberculosis, malignancy and oesophageal rupture.

E Abnormal pleural fluid LDH levels

LDH is used to differentiate an exudate from a transudate. Raised LDH is suggestive of an exudate and therefore infectious or inflammatory cause. It needs to be measured simultaneously with serum LDH as it is the ratio of pleural fluid to serum LDH that is interpreted. A ratio >0.6 indicates an exudate.

A Turbid fluid

Turbid fluid is suggestive of an infectious cause.

B High pleural fluid neutrophil count

This is also indicative of an infective cause.

D Abnormal liver function tests

Although deranged LFTs may suggest malignancy, there are other causes such as infection (particularly atypical organisms such as Legionella) and chronic disease such as liver cirrhosis.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old man attends for a chest X-ray as part of a medical prior to emigrating to Australia. Unfortunately the chest X-ray reveals a number of rounded opacities predominantly in the left lung field, all less than 3 cm in diameter. He has had 5 kg of unintentional weight loss over the past year but no other history of note.

Which of the following features would be the strongest pointer to malignancy when the chest X-ray is reviewed?
options: Spiculated margin to one of the nodules, with distortion of neighbouring vessels
A rounded appearance to the nodules
No enhancement with contrast on future CT thorax
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Spiculated margin to one of the nodules, with distortion of neighbouring vessels

A spiculated margin to one of the nodules, particularly when there is distortion of neighbouring vessels, raises the possibility of malignancy. Associated ground-glass shadowing, or the presence of cavitation or pseudo- cavitation within the lesion, increases the chances of malignant disease. CT thorax to further characterise the lesions is indicated.

D No enhancement with contrast on future CT thorax

Enhancement of nodules with contrast on CT thorax increases the likelihood that they are malignant in origin.

B Smaller lesion size

Lesions larger than 3 cm are more likely to be associated with underlying malignancy.

C A rounded appearance to the nodules

Rounded appearance to the nodules, implying organised growth, is less likely to be associated with an underlying malignancy.

E Age 62 at presentation

Older age at presentation and history of smoking are associated with increased likelihood of malignancy.

questions.question:
A 71-year-old patient undergoes radical surgery for an oesophageal adenocarcinoma with oesophagectomy, gastrectomy and splenectomy. Initially he makes a good recovery but you are asked to review him a few days later because he is increasingly short of breath. On examination BP is 142/72 mmHg and pulse 79/min and regular. There is reduced expansion of the left side of the chest and dullness to percussion over the left lung fields.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin109 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)7.9 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets172 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)139 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.2 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine105 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L

Chest X-ray Large left sided pleural effusion

Diagnostic tap milky coloured effusion, protein content 48g/L

Which of the following investigations on the pleural fluid is most likely to contribute to confirming the underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Triglycerides

A triglyceride level greater than 1.2 mmol/L indicates a 99% chance that the fluid in the pleural space is chyle. This is likely to be a complication of surgery, with intra-operative damage to the duct or one of its tributaries. This can cause up to 4 l of fluid per day to leak into the pleural space, leading to the classic symptoms of a large pleural effusion. Initial management is conservative as the thoracic duct leak reduces spontaneously over a few days. If the effusion persists, imaging is needed, with referral for surgical ligation as indicated.

C Culture and sensitivity

This would identify the organism in an infective pleural effusion but would not aid the diagnosis here.

B LDH

LDH is used to distinguish an exudate from a transudate, and is therefore utilised to elucidate the cause of pleural effusion when heart failure versus inflammation or infection needs to be delineated. It is often done as part of the routine tests on pleural fluid, but will not be the most useful in confirming the underlying diagnosis.

D pH

Testing the acidity of pleural fluid is used as a guide to treatment in para-pneumonic and malignant pleural effusions: a pH of <7.2 in the former indicates the need to drain, and <7.3 in the latter is associated with worse outcome. Neither is relevant in this clinical scenario.

E Glucose

Glucose levels are of value in para-pneumonic effusions and identify causes such as tuberculosis or malignancy.

questions.question:
A 54-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) attends for smoking cessation advice.

Which of the following methods is likely to be associated with the greatest chance of quitting?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Bupropion

Studies have shown success in smoking cessation in 20–30% of patients involved in bupropion studies at 1 year, with marginally higher quit rates seen when bupropion and nicotine replacement were combined (35%). Studies have shown that varenicline also aids smoking cessation in combination with motivational support, resulting in higher quit rates when higher doses were used (44% success rate).

E Hypnosis

Hypnosis aims to improve willpower in the subconscious state, and trials have showed no greater abstinence rate.

B Nicotine replacement lozenges

Nicotine replacement is associated with a quit rate of only around 10% in clinical trials.

C Willpower

Willpower quit rates are thought to be around only 2–4% at 1 year in reality.

D Nicotine replacement gum

Like option B, nicotine replacement is associated with a quit rate of only around 10% in clinical trials.

questions.question:
A 44-year-old man presented with a rash on his legs and feeling generally unwell with malaise, weight loss and fevers. He also had recently noticed some loss of sensation over the top of his right foot, with the foot- dragging when he walked. He had been diagnosed with asthma by his general practitioner many years ago and used a salbutamol inhaler as required. He also had a constant watery nasal discharge, but no epistaxis. He was a non-smoker.

On examination, he had low-grade pyrexia and scattered wheeze in his chest. Heart sounds were normal. His abdomen was soft and non-tender, with no masses. He had a purpuric rash on his lower limbs and several tender subcutaneous nodules on his forearms. He had a right foot drop but no other neurological abnormalities.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)106 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)10.9 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)390 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils6.2 ×10⁹/L1.5–7.0 ×10⁹/L
Eosinophils2.2 ×10⁹/L0.04–0.4 ×10⁹/L
Monocytes1.6 ×10⁹/L0.0–0.8 ×10⁹/L
Basophils0.1 ×10⁹/L< 0.1 ×10⁹/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)94 fl76–98 fl
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)82 mm/h1–20 mm/hour
Sodium (Na⁺)120 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.2 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)80 IU/L30–150 IU/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)30 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Urea5.2 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)42 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Bilirubin14 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)110 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Antinuclear antibody (ANA)Negative
Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (pANCA)Positive
UrinalysisNormal

His chest x-ray is shown below.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangitis

This man presents with the classic triad of asthma, eosinophilia and systemic vasculitis. There is usually a prodromal period for many years consisting of allergic rhinitis and late-onset asthma, which can be difficult to control.

The chest X-ray here shows pulmonary infiltrates bilaterally. Other findings occasionally found include nodules, transient hilar lymphadenopathy and pleural or pericardial effusions. Mononeuritis multiplex can occur. Anti- neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) is positive in approximately 40% of cases. Renal involvement is rare. Treatment is with high-dose corticosteroids, azathioprine or cyclophosphamide.

Image source: https://radiopaedia.org/cases/eosinophilic-granulomatosis-with-polyangiitis-3?lang=gb (https://radiopaedia.org/cases/eosinophilic-granulomatosis-with-polyangiitis-3?lang=gb)

A Systemic lupus erythematosus

Although SLE is associated with an erythematous rash on sun-exposed areas, the eosinophilia, negative ANA and positive pANCA would be unusual for a diagnosis of lupus.

B Polyarteritis nodosa

pANCA is classically not positive in patients with PAN. In addition, the symptoms of significant asthma poorly responsive to conventional therapies, and eosinophilia, are inconsistent with a diagnosis of PAN.

D Anti-GBM disease

This presents with rapidly progressive pulmonary and kidney disease, accompanied by haemoptysis and kidney disease due to glomerulonephritis. Eosinophilia isn’t a feature, nor is mononeuritis multiplex.

E Granulomatosis with polyangitis

This is associated with pulmonary and renal vasculitis with haemoptysis and a progressive rise in serum creatinine. There is usually sinusitis. cANCA rather than pANCA is more likely to be positive, and eosinophils are not elevated.

questions.question:
A 68-year-old man with a 10-year history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents with a 6- month history of increasing exertional dyspnoea and fatigue. He also has a cough productive of yellow sputum, episodes of chest pain, nausea and anorexia. He stopped smoking 2 years ago.

On examination, he had raised jugular venous pressure (JVP), right parasternal heave, a loud second heart sound and an ejection systolic murmur at the left second intercostal space. On chest auscultation, he had scattered expiratory wheeze and bi-basal crepitations. He had pitting leg oedema.

Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)180 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)8.0 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)220 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)135 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.2 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)110 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Bilirubin16 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L
Urea4.6 mmol/L2.5–6.5 mmol/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)50 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Gamma-glutamyltransferase (γGT)100 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Electrocardiogram (ECG)Right ventricular hypertrophy, peaked P waves

Chest X-ray (CXR) Shown below

Which of the following therapies is most likely to improve long-term prognosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Long-term oxygen therapy

This man has developed cor pulmonale, which is defined as right heart failure secondary to pulmonary hypertension. Causes include any chronic lung disease, pulmonary vascular disease, hypoventilation neuromuscular disorders and thoracic cage abnormalities. Long-term home oxygen therapy for at least 15 hours per day can reduce hypoxia, which lowers pulmonary resistance and can improve symptoms and increase life expectancy.

C Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor

In contrast to left ventricular impairment, ACE inhibitors do not have any prognostic benefit and may, in fact, make matters worse. In systolic heart failure, they are of prognostic benefit and very useful.

A High-dose furosemide

Diuretics can be used for right ventricular failure, but care should be taken to avoid excessive fluid depletion. In heart failure, these do not improve long-term prognosis.

D Regular venesection

This patient has polycythaemia secondary to chronic hypoxia as a mechanism of compensation. Venesection improves prognosis in haemochromatosis and can also be used for primary polycythaemia.

E Daily amoxicillin

There is no role for antibiotic prophylaxis in either cor pulmonale or COPD.

questions.question:
You are called to a cardiac arrest on the coronary care unit. A 74-year-old woman with a 40-pack year smoking history and COPD on high-dose salmeterol/fluticasone combination inhaler has arrested two days after admission with an inferior myocardial infarction.

Arterial blood gasses on admission reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
pH7.397.35–7.45
pO₂8.5 mmol/L10.5–13.5 kPa
pCO₂5.8 mmol/L4.6–6.0 kPa
HCO₃⁻31 mmol/L24–30 mmol/L

Arterial blood gasses on 35% O₂ post-cardiac arrest reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
pH7.297.35–7.45
pO₂7.5 kPa10.5–13.5 kPa
pCO₂6.9 kPa4.6–6.0 kPa

She responds appropriately to commands and is cooperative and conscious around 15 min after her cardiac arrest. A portable chest X-ray is shown below.

Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action with respect to her ventilatory support?
options: Consider her for non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV)
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Consider her for non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV)

On admission her arterial blood gasses revealed a compensated respiratory acidosis with some degree of CO₂ retention. Post cardiac arrest she has decompensated with relative hypoxia and CO₂ retention. At this point the concern is that the acidosis may promote further respiratory weakness, driving CO₂ retention and worsening the pH further. NIPPV should reverse the respiratory acidosis and may have a positive impact on any pulmonary oedema associated with the MI. The chest x-ray shows hyperinflation, in keeping with COPD, and an absence of any sign of resuscitation injury.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:COPD.JPG (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:COPD.JPG)

C Increase her inspired oxygen to 60%

This, like continuing 35% O₂, risks worsening respiratory acidosis without significantly increasing PaO₂ because of consequent respiratory muscle weakness and steadily decreasing consciousness.

A Continue 35% O₂ therapy

Continuing her 35% O₂ may further exacerbate CO₂ retention and lead to respiratory arrest, because of increasing drowsiness and lethargy.

B Reduce her inspired oxygen to 28%

This risks worsening any hypoxia, which could exacerbate myocardial ischaemia leading to chest pain and/or rhythm disturbance.

E Move to intubation and ventilation

This should be carefully considered based on pre-morbid status, and ideally would be a step only after NIPPV had not succeeded in maintaining oxygenation and reversing respiratory acidosis.

questions.question:
A 41-year-old woman who is known to have brittle asthma was admitted to the Emergency Department with increased shortness of breath and a severe cough over the past few days, productive of yellow/green sputum. She was pyrexial 38.4°C, pulse was 90/min and regular, BP was 85/60 mmHg on admission, but improved with a fluid challenge. You review her on the ward some 36 h later, with her blood culture results. Her BP is now 105/70 mmHg, with pulse 75/min and regular. There are right basal crackles consistent with consolidation. She is still spiking fevers of 39.2°C every few hours.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)129 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)15.2×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)203 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
C-reactive protein (CRP)215 mg/L< 10 mg/L
Sodium (Na⁺)132 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)5.1 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)162 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
Urea14.1 mmol/L2.5 - 6.5 mmol/L
Blood culturesPseudomonas

Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic choice?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D IV tazocin

The choice here is between oral quinolone and IV therapy for Pseudomonas. Given that this patient is still spiking fevers and has an elevated urea, IV therapy with tazocin is most appropriate.

A IV colistin (polymyxin E)

Colistin is generally reserved for serious pseudomonal infections that are resistant to therapy with other agents.

B IV gentamicin

Gentamicin monotherapy is not recommended for the treatment of respiratory tract infections.

C IV meropenem

Carbapenems are an option for the treatment of Pseudomonas, although inducible resistance is a concern. For this reason, tazocin is the preferred option.

E Oral ciprofloxacin

Although oral ciprofloxacin is an option for pseudomonal infection, the severity of this patient’s pneumonia drives us more towards IV tazocin as the preferred therapy. It is also now recommended that quinolone treatment is avoided wherever an effective alternative is available due to a small but significant risk of debilitating adverse effects. 70490

questions.question:
A 27-year-old woman presents with right-sided pleuritic chest pain. She says the pain came on suddenly while lifting her son into his push-chair some 30 h earlier. Her only medication of note is the oral contraceptive pill, and she is usually fit and well. The symptoms have largely resolved and she has not taken paracetamol for some 6 h. On examination, BP is 120/70 mmHg, pulse 80/min and regular, breath sounds seem normal and O₂ saturation on air is 97%.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin129 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)8.2 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets192 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)138 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.3 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine110 µmol/L Small right pneumothorax50–120 µmol/L

Chest X-ray – rim less than 1cm

Which of the following is the most appropriate next course of action?
options: Send home with a plan for early review
Admit for observation and oxygen therapy
Admit for formal chest drain insertion
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Send home with a plan for early review

This woman has a pneumothorax which is more than 1 day old, and the chest X-ray indicates that the size is small. Given that her symptoms are improving, it would be most appropriate to discharge her with a plan to review in the respiratory clinic, or to return if her pain significantly worsens. Air aspiration might be considered for a larger pneumothorax, whereas formal chest drain insertion would be indicated if the pneumothorax was larger and there was a previous history of chest disease.

E Admit for thoracoscopy

Thoracoscopy is usually performed to investigate pleural disease or in preparation for pleurodesis. This patient has had a spontaneous pneumothorax and there is no current suspicion of underlying lung disease. The annual incidence of primary spontaneous pneumothorax is around 5/100,000 in women and around 25/100,000 in men. The greatest risk factor is smoking.

B Admit for observation and oxygen therapy

The patient’s oxygen saturations are 97% on air, so there is no indication for supplemental oxygen. As this is a spontaneous pneumothorax in an otherwise well patient

C Admit for air aspiration

In the case of a primary spontaneous pneumothorax, air aspiration is only indicated if the pneumothorax is >2 cm and/or the patient is breathless. If this fails to resolve the symptoms or the pneumothorax does not decrease in size, then formal chest drain insertion would be needed.

D Admit for formal chest drain insertion

Formal chest drain insertion is only indicated in symptomatic/>2 cm primary spontaneous pneumothorax where aspiration has failed. It is first line if there is underlying lung disease and the patient is breathless or the pneumothorax is >2 cm in size.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old dairy farmer attends the Respiratory Clinic with shortness of breath, chronic cough, lethargy and night sweats. He has a history of type II diabetes, for which he takes metformin. Apparently, the farm has had financial troubles over the past few months because of the need to cull approximately 50% of the herd due to tuberculosis (TB). On examination, his BP is 135/75 mmHg and his heart rate is 75 bpm and regular. His BMI is 35 kg/m 2. He has wheeze on auscultation of the chest, as well as a few scattered coarse crackles.

Pulmonary function testing (PFT) reveals a mild restrictive defect.

His CXR is shown below:

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D Miliary TB

This patient has symptoms of chronic lung disease, and the CXR shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Given the fact that the patient has been exposed to TB, this is most likely to indicate miliary TB. The diagnosis should be confirmed with at least three sputum samples, and given the extent of the infection, contact tracing and testing

are essential.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Chest_radiograph_of_miliary_tuberculosis_1.jpg

E Obesity hypoventilation syndrome

This is associated with a mild restrictive defect on PFT but not with nodular shadowing on the CXR, nor with the auscultation findings seen in this patient.

A Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis

This leads to an obstructive picture on PFT and symptoms consistent with poorly controlled asthma. Patchy shadowing is usually apparent on the CXR rather than the nodular appearance seen in this patient.

B Asthma

Asthma is more likely to be associated with a normal appearance on the CXR and would not fit with other constitutional symptoms of infection, including lethargy and night sweats seen here.

C Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

This would be associated with a restrictive defect on PFT, although coarse crepitations and nodular appearance on the CXR would not be expected. Patchy shadowing on the chest X-ray and inspiratory crepitations would be expected.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department drowsy and confused. He has recently complained of symptoms of an upper respiratory tract infection. He has a past medical history of Duchenne’s muscular dystrophy. Over the past few weeks, he noted that he seemed to be suffering intermittent morning headaches and intermittent confusion. On examination, he is drowsy but able to obey simple commands. His respiratory rate is 13 breaths per minute. Air entry is poor on auscultation, with crackles at the left base.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
pH7.37.35–7.45
pCO₂7.0 kPa4.6–6.0 kPa
pO₂7.0 kPa10.5–13.5 kPa

Which of the following would represent the most appropriate management in this case?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Non-invasive ventilation

This man has evidence of chronic carbon dioxide retention, as evidenced by his morning headaches, intermittent confusion and drowsiness. A further indication of respiratory muscle, particularly diaphragmatic and weakness may be indicated by breathlessness during swimming. Chronic hypoventilation has likely led to an opportunistic respiratory tract infection associated with his cold. At present, he has mild respiratory acidosis, and the situation may be remediable with non-invasive ventilation and antibiotics. Since Duchenne's muscular dystrophy is progressive, intubation and ventilation should be carefully considered.

A 60% oxygen therapy

Therapy with 60% oxygen will have a very limited impact, if any, on improving this patient’s hypoxia due to his hypoventilation and worsening acidosis. Therefore, this is not an appropriate option for this patient.

B 35% oxygen therapy

Like higher percentages of oxygen, 35% oxygen will not reverse the impact of hypoventilation with respect to respiratory acidosis. Therefore, it would not be appropriate here.

C 28% oxygen therapy

Therapy with 28% oxygen will not improve oxygenation and will not reverse the impact of hypoventilation, making it unlikely to be appropriate for this patient.

D Intubation and ventilation

Intubation and ventilation should be carefully considered in the context of Duchenne’s muscular dystrophy. It is a progressive condition and the risk is that the patient may become un-weanable from the ventilator. As such, non-invasive ventilation is preferred here. Ideally, patients should consider an advanced directive before they become unwell so that their wishes with respect to invasive therapies are already established. 18554

questions.question:
A 64-year-old woman comes to the Respiratory Clinic for review. She has recently been diagnosed with moderate COPD and is about to commence therapy for the condition. She also has a history of hypertension and chronic stable angina for which she receives ramipril, indapamide and diltiazem. On examination her BP is 132/82 mmHg, with pulse 70/min and regular. There is bilateral poor air entry with quiet wheeze on auscultation of the chest.

Which of the following is likely to have the greatest short-term impact on her quality of life, (in the next 2-3 months)?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Pulmonary rehabilitation

Pulmonary rehabilitation has been shown to improve exercise tolerance in COPD, and will also improve this patient’s exercise tolerance in relation to her chronic stable angina. Over a relatively short time, (about 6-8 weeks), these improvements have been shown to lead to quality of life (QoL) benefit.

E Tiotropium

Although tiotropium did show an impact on the St George’s respiratory quality of life score, the effect was moderate and was only seen in 3 out of 4 pivotal studies. Hence over the short term, pulmonary rehabilitation carries greater benefit.

A Ipratropium

Short-acting anti-cholinergics do not significantly impact on quality of life in COPD.

B Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT)

LTOT reduces progression of pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure over the longer term. Although this translates into QoL benefit over the longer term, in the short term pulmonary rehabilitation will have a greater impact.

D Salbutamol

Short acting beta-agonists do not have significant impact on QoL in COPD.

questions.question:
A woman presents to clinic in her eighth week of pregnancy. She is concerned about her husband’s family history of cystic fibrosis (CF), as her husband’s brother has cystic fibrosis and her husband has been confirmed as a carrier. The patient does not wish to know about her risk of developing CF and is reluctant to be tested herself, but is concerned about the health of her child. There is a 1:20 prevalence of CF carriage in the area where she lived as a child and husband and wife are not consanguineous.

What is the chance of her child having cystic fibrosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C 1/80

CF is an autosomal recessive disease, so two abnormal alleles are required for the disease to be manifest. As a carrier (with one abnormal gene) the husband has a 1:2 chance of passing the abnormal gene to his offspring.
