C Aspergillus-specific IgE radioallergosorbant (RAST) level

Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) should always be excluded in people with asthma who have a raised eosinophil count. ABPA is a hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus in people with asthma. This can be done by sputum culture or testing for atopy to the fungi with RAST, skin-prick tests or IgE specific to the fungi. Aspergillus precipitins testing looks for the presence of the antibody in the serum; if the result is highly positive, the patient may have invasive aspergillosis.

E Stool culture for ova, cysts and parasites

Stool culture may be positive in a parasitic cause of eosinophilia pneumonia, but this is unlikely given the very minor chest X-ray changes.

A Antinuclear antibody (ANA)

Although eosinophil count can also be raised in Churg–Strauss syndrome, a small-to-medium-vessel vasculitis that presents usually in adults with asthma-like symptoms, this results in a positive pANCA, not ANA.

B IgE

A high eosinophil count may be due to her atopy and the high pollen count, so her total IgE would also be raised.

D Peak flow reading

Peak flow readings will likely be low in respiratory diseases like asthma, ABPA and Churg–Strauss, and therefore not good at excluding causes of wheeze and exacerbation.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old man who has a history of COPD, for which he takes fluticasone and salmeterol (combined) and salbutamol, comes to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset shortness of breath and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. He takes a number of medications for hypertension and ischaemic heart disease, but has recently enrolled on a pulmonary rehabilitation programme and is walking up to 2 miles per day. On examination, his BP is 155/90 mmHg with heart rate of 92 bpm and regular. He has diminished breath sounds over the right-hand side on auscultation. Oxygen saturation is reduced at 90%. CXR reveals a right-sided pneumothorax with a 1.5 cm rim of air.

Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
options: Discharge and review in two weeks
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Insert size 8–14 Fr chest drain

In a patient with a symptomatic pneumothorax, intervention is warranted. Where there are high risk characteristics (i.e. unstable patient, tension pneumothorax, bilateral pneumothorax, underlying lung disease, >50 years old with significant smoking history and haemopneumothorax) a chest drain is preferred to air aspiration and is therefore the correct course of action.

D Discharge and review in two weeks

This is the correct course of action after successful treatment of a pneumothorax.

A Admit for oxygen

While this was previously the the correct course of action after successful air aspiration for a secondary pneumothorax, BTS guidelines have changed. Oxygen should be provided for any patient who is hypoxic, although a chest drain is additionally warranted here.

B Air aspiration

Air aspiration, an ambulatory device or conservative management can be undertaken for any symptomatic patient who has no high risk characteristics, depending on patient preference.

C Discharge and review in 24 hours

Discharge and review in 2–4 weeks is recommended where conservative management is appropriate or following a procedure to reduce a pneumothorax.

questions.question:
A 36-year-old man presents with increasing shortness of breath and a cough, which is worse at night. He has no significant past medical history. He has never smoked. He works as a car mechanic, restoring run-down cars. He notes that his symptoms are often better at the weekend.

Investigations:

InvestigationResult
FEV170% of normal
FVC85% of normal
PEFR450 l/min
Histamine challenge test20% fall in FEV1 with 2 micromol/l histamine (normal >4)

What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Occupational asthma

This man has occupational asthma secondary to isocyanates, which are found in paints used to spray cars. Occupational asthma is characterised by airway obstruction and/or bronchial hyper-reactivity induced by a person’s occupation. His spirometry reveals an obstructive picture with a hyper-responsive histamine challenge test. Diagnosis is confirmed by asking the patient to do 2 h peak flows both at his place of work and at home, and ideally during a period of leave from work, to look for significant differences and worsening of PEFR at work.

Other occupations commonly associated with occupational asthma that may come up in the MRCP exam include: bakers, vets, hairdressers, pharmaceutical workers, welders, roofers and textile workers. Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Normal_AP.JPG

D Extrinsic Allergic Alveolitis

There is no history of allergen exposure to suggest EAA, which usually presents as a flu-like illness with dyspnoea soon after exposure to the offending allergen. The chest x-ray in EAA can be normal, especially in early disease, with later disease showing fibrosis, typically of the upper lobes, volume loss and cardiomegaly.

A Carbon monoxide poisoning

The chest x-ray in carbon monoxide poisoning is usually normal, as here, however imaging can sometimes show a ground-glass appearance and alveolar oedema. It would usually present as a flu-like illness with malaise and fatigue, unlike in this case. There can be dyspnoea on exertion and chest pain with palpitations can occur. As exposure progresses, lethargy, hallucinations, agitation and confusion occur, eventually leading to coma. Patients may also experience headache, abdominal pain with nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea.

C Silicosis

Silicosis is associated with occupations such as foundry work, hard rock mining and civil engineering, and is due to inhalation of silicon dioxide. The history does not suggest this and the chest x-ray usually shows upper lobe fibrosis, unlike the normal film seen here.

E Hyperactive airways

The patient does have hyperactive airways, but the 20% drop in FEV 1 on histamine challenge confirms a diagnosis of asthma as the underlying cause.

questions.question:
A 37-year-old Afro-Caribbean woman presents to the Emergency Department with a painful raised rash affecting both shins. She has been followed up on a number of occasions over the past few months by her General Practitioner because of complaints of shortness of breath and a dry cough. This has not responded to a salbutamol inhaler or two courses of amoxicillin. There is no past medical history of note. On examination, her blood pressure is 145/89 mmHg; pulse is 75 bpm and regular. Her chest is clear on auscultation, and her abdomen is soft and non-tender. There is a rash on both shins consistent with erythema nodosum.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)131 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)9.1 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)178 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)138 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.5 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)103 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Corrected calcium (Ca)2.71 mmol/L2.2–2.6 mmol/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)33 IU/L5–30 IU/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)95 IU/L30–130 IU/L
Bilirubin11 µmol/L2–17 µmol/L

Which of the following investigations should be performed next?
options: Sputum for microscopy, culture and sensitivity
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Chest X-ray

Given the patients ethnicity, symptoms of shortness of breath and a rash consistent with erythema nodosum. The next logical step would be a chest X-ray given the suspicions of a possible diagnosis of sarcoidosis. CT thorax and pulmonary function tests can be used to confirm the diagnosis. Controversy exists over the role of steroids in the short term; however, it has been widely seen that there is some symptom reduction and a chest X-ray therefore may be indicated.

D Sputum for microscopy, culture and sensitivity

The clinical presentation would be consistent with a patient suspected of sarcoidosis. Sputum for microscopy, culture and sensitivity would not be indicated.

A Autoimmune profile

Patients with erythema nodosum may require autoimmune profiling; however, the clinical scenario is more in keeping with a diagnosis of sarcoidosis. Therefore, an autoimmune profile is not clinically indicated.

B Computed tomography (CT) thorax

The patient’s clinical features would suggest a diagnosis of sarcoidosis. A chest X-ray would be able to confirm the presence of lymphadenopathy. CT thorax is used to confirm the diagnosis and identify areas of possible fibrosis; it is not the most useful next investigation.

E Ultrasound scan (USS) abdomen

Although the liver function tests are mildly elevated, it would not be appropriate next best investigation. The clinical scenario indicates a possible diagnosis of sarcoidosis and therefore a chest X-ray is the most logical next investigation.

questions.question:
A 64-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with nausea, vomiting and polyuria over the past few days. By the time he reaches the hospital he is drowsy and confused. Past medical history of note includes COPD, for which he takes high-dose seretide, a previous anterior myocardial infarction (MI), and he continues to smoke 30 cigarettes per day. On examination his BP is 115/75 mmHg, with pulse 90/min and regular. There is bilateral poor air entry on auscultation of the chest, with quiet wheeze. Abdomen is soft and non-tender.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Haemoglobin (Hb)131 g/L135 - 175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)9.2 ×10⁹/L4.0 - 11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)203 ×10⁹/L150 - 400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)145 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)5.1 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)151 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L
Glucose6.9 mmol/L3.9 - 7.1 mmol/L
Corrected calcium (Ca²⁺)3.31 mmol/L2.2 - 2.7 mmol/L
Albumin38 g/L35 - 55 g/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)122 u/L7 - 55 u/L
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)191 u/L30 - 150 u/L
Phosphate (PO₄³⁻)0.7 mmol/L1.1 - 1.45 mmol/L

Chest x-ray shown below.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Small cell carcinoma of the bronchus
Squamous cell carcinoma of the bronchus
questions.explanation:
Explanation

E Squamous cell carcinoma of the bronchus

The chest x-ray reveals a peripheral mass in the left upper lobe. The most likely diagnosis in this case with hypercalcaemia and phosphate below the lower limit of the normal range, is squamous cell carcinoma of the bronchus associated with production of parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP). If intact PTH is measured,

then this is found to be below the lower limit of normal.

Image source: https://radiopaedia.org/cases/cavitating-lung-cancer?lang=gb

A Adenocarcinoma of the bronchus

Bronchial adenocarcinoma is rarely associated with paraneoplastic syndromes, although some cases of polymyositis are documented.

B Bronchial carcinoid

Bronchial carcinoid generally occurs at a younger age and is not associated with smoking; lesions are often peripheral. It is most likely to be associated with secretion of serotonin, although tumours secreting ACTH and growth hormone are also seen.

C Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma

In NHL more extensive lymphadenopathy would be expected, and although PTHrP secretion is seen in NHL, it is much less frequently seen than in bronchial carcinoma.

D Small cell carcinoma of the bronchus

This is more likely to be associated with syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH) and hyponatraemia.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old man with known emphysema presented to the Emergency Department with sudden onset of severe right-sided pleuritic chest pain and shortness of breath. He is a smoker of 20/day. On examination he looks unwell. He is pale and sweaty. BP 140/85 mmHg, pulse 120/min, respiratory rate 30/min, SaO₂ 88% on air. He has reduced expansion and reduced breath sounds on the right side. Heart sounds were normal and abdominal examination unremarkable.

ABGs on air:

InvestigationResult
pH7.41
PO₂7.5 kPa
PCO₂6.5 kPa

His CXR is shown below;

He is given 28% oxygen and analgesia and his saturations improve.

What would your immediate management of this patient be?
options: Insertion of an intercostal chest drain
Arrange an urgent CT scan of the chest
Insertion of an intercostal tube and apply suction
questions.explanation:
Explanation

B Insertion of an intercostal chest drain

This man has a secondary pneumothorax as he has underlying lung disease. The management is different for primary (no underlying pulmonary disease) and secondary (underlying pulmonary disease) pneumothoraces. Current guidelines 1 suggest that an intercostal drain should be inserted if the patient is breathless, over 50 years old with a significant smoking history and there is a rim of air of > 2 cm from the chest wall on a standard size chest X-ray. This patient fits all the above criteria.

Suction should not be applied immediately and it is recommended that it should not be routinely employed. It maybe considered after 48 hours whilst awaiting surgical review if the lung is not fully re-expanded or if there is a persistent air leak. Suction should be low-pressure (-10 to -20 cmH 2O), high-volume.

If this patient had a persistent air leak, despite suction, they should be referred to the thoracic surgeons. The exact timing of referral remains contentious but it is suggested that in cases of persistent air leak or failure of the lung to re-expand, an early (3-5 days) thoracic surgical opinion should be sought. For secondary pneumothoraces, an early thoracic surgical referral is recommended.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:PNTX.png

D Refer to the thoracic surgeons

It would be appropriate to try and resolve pneumothorax with an intercostal drain before assessing whether a surgical referral is required.

A Chest aspiration

Chest aspiration should only be considered for a secondary pneumothorax <2cm if the patient is clinically stable.

C Arrange an urgent CT scan of the chest

A CT is not required here, the diagnosis of pneumothorax is clearly visible on CXR.

E Insertion of an intercostal tube and apply suction

Suction should be applied with caution due to risk of re-expansion pulmonary oedema. It should only be applied after consideration and specialist advice and monitoring.

questions.question:
You are seeing a patient in clinic. Unfortunately, all clinic notes in the Cardiorespiratory Test Department, are being audited; however, the patient brings along a copy of her lung function results. Her date of birth is missing from the report.

Lung function results reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal value
FEV10.301.2–2.9
Total lung capacity6.84.4–6.8
Corrected transfer factor3.44.2–8.8

From these results, which disease do you suspect that she is most likely to have?
options: Very severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
questions.explanation:
Explanation

A Very severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)

COPD is defined as a reduced FEV 1/FVC ratio (where FEV 1 is forced expired volume in 1 second and FVC is forced vital capacity), such that FEV 1/FVC is less than 0.7. Though you are not given an FVC reading, note that the total lung capacity here is within the normal range, yet the FEV 1 is significantly reduced, this fits best with a diagnosis of COPD.

D Non-specific interstitial pneumonitis (NSIP)

Restrictive lung disease is associated with a decreased total lung capacity.

B Severe asthma

Asthma is associated with a normal or raised transfer factor.

C Moderate COPD

Predicted FEV1 in moderate COPD is 50–79%. See table below for classification of COPD.

FEV1 % predictedSeverity of airflow obstruction
> 80%Mild**
50–79%Moderate
30–49%Severe
< 30%Very severe

**If FEV1 is ≥ 80% predicted normal, a diagnosis of COPD should only be made in the presence of respiratory symptoms, for example breathlessness or cough.

FEV 1 % predicted Severity of airflow obstruction

> 80% Mild**

50–79% Moderate

30–49% Severe

< 30% Very severe **If FEV 1 is ≥ 80% predicted normal, a diagnosis of COPD should only be made in the presence of respiratory symptoms, for example breathlessness or cough.

E Sarcoidosis

Like NSIP, sarcoidosis falls under the category of restrictive lung disease, and is associated with a decreased total lung capacity.

A 62-year-old man is admitted to hospital with a 3-day history of dyspnoea, pleuritic chest pain and several episodes of haemoptysis.

Before this, he described several months of constant rhinorrhoea, with some nasal crusting, several large epistaxes and constant pain below his eyes. More recently, he had noticed some double vision and swelling of his right eye.

On examination, he had low-grade pyrexia and was normotensive. There was some nasal mucosal ulceration and right-sided proptosis. Cardiovascular examination was unremarkable. He had localised areas of crepitations throughout both lung fields. His abdomen was soft and non-tender, with no masses. There were no focal neurological signs or skin lesions.

Investigation results are below:

What would be the most useful investigation in pointing to the diagnosis if positive?
options: High-resolution computed tomography (CT) scan of the thorax
questions.explanation:
Explanation

C Serum antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies

This patient has the typical features of Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), which is a necrotising granulomatous arteritis of the upper and lower respiratory tract and kidney. It is rare, with an incidence of 5–10 per million. It is a multisystem disease and may affect the eyes, skin, joints, heart and nervous system. Pulmonary involvement is seen in 95% of cases, and renal involvement in 85% of cases. A positive serum antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) is present in > 90% of cases of GPA and strongly supports the diagnosis. Renal biopsy is sometimes required.

Treatment is with steroids and cyclophosphamide. Untreated, 1-year mortality is 80%, but with appropriate therapy, remission can be achieved in up to 90% of patients.

B Serum anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) antibodies

This scenario is not anti-GBM disease; therefore, these antibodies will be normal. Anti-GBM disease typically causes macroscopic haematuria & proteinuria with mild renal impairment along with alveolar haemorrhage.

A High-resolution computed tomography (CT) scan of the thorax

This may show the cavitating lung lesions in more detail but will not aid in the diagnosis.

D Serum antinuclear antibodies

Serum antinuclear antibodies will not aid in the diagnosis.

E Urine microscopy

Urine microscopy may show blood and protein; however, it is non-specific for the diagnosis.

A 71-year-old white man is admitted to your ward with a 3-day history of pleuritic right-sided chest pain, cough productive of green sputum, shortness of breath and a fever. He has smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 50 years and is usually fit and well. He has no penicillin allergy.

On examination, he is alert, has a fever of 38.1 °C and a respiratory rate of 40/min. He is tachycardic, pulse 120/min and his blood pressure is 86/61 mmHg. On chest auscultation, he has coarse inspiratory breath sounds and bronchial breathing in the right lower lobe.

Investigations:

InvestigationResultNormal value
Sodium (Na⁺)131 mmol/L135 - 145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)4.2 mmol/L3.5 - 5.0 mmol/L
Urea14.2 mmol/L2.5 - 6.5 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)137 µmol/L50 - 120 µmol/L

Chest X-ray shows shadowing in the right lower zone and blunting of the right heart border.

You want to start this patient on medication for his pneumonia.

Which of the following antibiotics/antibiotic combinations would be a reasonable choice for treatment?
options: Oral co-amoxiclav 625 mg tds + oral clarithromycin 500 mg bd
IV levofloxacin 500 mg od and oral rifampicin 600 mg od
IV co-amoxiclav 1.2 g tds and PO clarithromycin 500mg BD
questions.explanation:
Explanation

D IV co-amoxiclav 1.2 g tds and PO clarithromycin 500mg BD

This patient has severe community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) as defined by a CURB 65 score of 4. British Thoracic Society (BTS) guidelines have recommended that all patients with pneumonia are assessed using CURB 65. Where possible clarithromycin should be given orally due to the risk of phlebitis with IV route.

Patients get 1 point each for

confusion

urea >7 mmol/L respiratory rate >30/min blood pressure <90 mmHg systolic and 60 mmHg diastolic and patient older than 65.

Scores 3+ indicate high mortality.

Treatment for severe CAP is of course driven by local antibiotic protocols but an acceptable choice of antibiotics would be the combination of co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin delivered IV as a first-line option.

C IV levofloxacin 500 mg od and oral rifampicin 600 mg od

Rifampicin can be added if a staphylococcal cause of pneumonia is suspected.

A 2019 UK government drug safety update advises that fluoroquinolones should now be avoided in mild to moderate infections unless other commonly recommended antibiotics are not suitable. This is due to rare reports of long lasting or potentially irreversible side effects such as tendinitis and peripheral neuropathy. Fluoroquinolones should be used with special caution in patients older than 60 years or those with renal impairment; treatment should be discontinued promptly at fist signs of serious adverse reactions.

A IV cefuroxime 1.5 g tds

IV cefuroxime can be used for severe sepsis with oral clarithromycin if the patient is penicillin allergic.

B Oral co-amoxiclav 625 mg tds + oral clarithromycin 500 mg bd

This treatment option could be considered for mild to moderate community-acquired pneumonia if amoxicillin had recently been used and shown to be ineffective.

E IV ciprofloxacin 400 mg bd

Ciprofloxacin is effective against Pseudomonas but has little use in the empirical treatment of CAP.
